ask.changes_what: Present: escalate now - CT angiography for suspected mesenteric ischemia; urgent surgical consult for suspected necrotizing infection. Absent: does not lower probability enough to stop work-up.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not apply to patients who cannot report pain reliably (sedation, dementia, spinal cord injury); absence of the sign never excludes either diagnosis.
ask.escalation_warning: Suspected necrotizing infection or mesenteric ischemia is time-critical: surgical consultation / CT angiography without waiting for laboratory results.

evidence.citation: Alayed KA, Tan C, Daneman N. Red Flags for Necrotizing Fasciitis: A Case Control Study. International journal of infectious diseases : IJID : official publication of the International Society for Infectious Diseases. 2016.
evidence.population: All NF cases admitted to a large Canadian tertiary hospital 2004-2013, each matched to two cellulitis controls (retrospective case-control)
evidence.quote: The clinical features that most significantly increased the odds of NF were recent surgery (LR+ 7.0) pain-out-of-proportion (LR+ 4.5), diarrhea (LR+ 6.0)
evidence.reference_standard: Admitted with diagnosis of necrotizing fasciitis (chart-confirmed) versus cellulitis controls
evidence.target_condition: Necrotizing fasciitis versus cellulitis (case-control): pain-out-of-proportion documented on history/physical examination

ask.how: Compare reported pain severity and analgesic requirement with objective findings: for the abdomen, severe continuous pain with a soft, non-tender or minimally tender abdomen; for skin/soft tissue, severe pain or exquisite tenderness extending beyond the visible erythema, or pain disproportionate to a modest cellulitis. Record the discordance explicitly.
ask.negative_finding: Absence is not reassuring: no single red flag had sufficient sensitivity to rule out necrotizing fasciitis (LR- >=0.5 for all findings), and mesenteric ischemia frequently presents with vague or non-specific pain, especially in the elderly.
ask.pitfalls: Late presentations of ischemia develop peritonism, so the sign is transient; analgesia, diabetes, and altered mental status blunt reporting. Distinguishing 'out of proportion' is subjective and undefined in most studies.
ask.positive_finding: In a soft-tissue infection, pain out of proportion raised the odds of necrotizing fasciitis about 4.5-fold versus cellulitis in a case-control study; in abdominal pain with vascular risk (AF, atherosclerosis, low flow), it is the classic cue for early mesenteric ischemia and should prompt CT angiography rather than observation.
ask.prerequisites: Patient able to report pain; opioid or sedative effect accounted for.
ask.rationale: Pain out of proportion is a key discriminator for necrotizing fasciitis and should prompt urgent escalation if present.
ask.title: Pain out of proportion to examination findings

ask.changes_what: Positive items push the Wells score toward moderate/high: order compression ultrasound (or CTPA) rather than relying on D-dimer alone; negative items lower the score and enable D-dimer exclusion.
ask.do_not_use_when: Do not use individual risk factors alone to exclude VTE; do not apply Wells-based D-dimer exclusion to inpatients, pregnant patients, or those already anticoagulated, where the derivation cohorts do not apply.
ask.escalation_warning: Hypotension, syncope or hypoxia with any VTE risk factor mandates immediate imaging or empiric anticoagulation, not D-dimer triage.

ask.how: Ask directly: bed rest >=3 days or major surgery within the past 4-12 weeks; any previous DVT or PE confirmed by imaging; cancer treated within 6 months or palliative. Record each item separately for the Wells DVT or PE score rather than as a global impression.
ask.negative_finding: Absence of individual risk factors does not exclude VTE; a low Wells score (LR ~0.25) plus a negative D-dimer is what allows exclusion without imaging.
ask.pitfalls: Risk-factor LRs were pooled from heterogeneous cohorts and are weaker in patients with prior VTE. Malignancy and prior VTE also raise D-dimer, so they do not license D-dimer-only exclusion in high-probability patients.
ask.positive_finding: Any single risk factor raises the probability of DVT only modestly (pooled LR+ about 1.8-2.7); the value comes from combining items in a Wells score, where a high score carries LR ~5.
ask.prerequisites: Patient or collateral historian able to give a reliable history; check the chart for prior imaging-confirmed VTE and oncology history.
ask.rationale: VTE risk factors help assess the likelihood of DVT, which is an important alternative diagnosis in acute unilateral leg swelling.
ask.title: VTE risk history (Wells items): immobilization >=3 days or surgery within 4-12 weeks, prior objectively confirmed VTE, active malignancy

examine.changes_what: Any hard sign should move necrotizing infection to the top of the differential and prompt urgent surgical exploration; their absence must not be used to de-escalate.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay surgical consultation to complete serial examinations when hard signs are already present.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never use absence of hard signs (or a low LRINEC) to rule out necrotizing infection in a patient with severe pain, toxicity or rapid progression.
examine.escalation_warning: Hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, skin anesthesia, hypotension or spread beyond the marked border require immediate surgical consultation and broad-spectrum antibiotics; delay to debridement increases mortality.

examine.how: Fully expose the limb/trunk and inspect for bullae (especially hemorrhagic or violaceous), dusky or necrotic skin; palpate for crepitus and for tenderness or induration extending beyond visible erythema; test light-touch sensation over the affected skin. Mark the erythema border with pen and time, and re-examine within 1-2 h for spread.
examine.negative_finding: Absence of any single hard sign does not exclude necrotizing infection: pooled sensitivity is 0.25 for bullae, 0.21 for hypotension and 0.46 for fever.
examine.pitfalls: Hard signs are late; pain out of proportion, tachycardia and systemic toxicity precede them. Crepitus is present only with gas-forming organisms, and anesthesia can be masked by analgesia or neuropathy (diabetes).
examine.positive_finding: Hemorrhagic bullae (pooled specificity 0.958) or hypotension (0.977) in a soft tissue infection strongly favors necrotizing infection and should trigger immediate surgical consultation; crepitus, anesthesia and rapid spread are treated the same way by consensus.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate exposure and analgesia; a documented baseline border and time for serial comparison.
examine.rationale: Hard signs of necrotizing infection require immediate surgical evaluation and can be life-saving if identified early.
examine.title: Necrotizing infection hard signs: hemorrhagic bullae, crepitus, skin anesthesia, spread beyond marked border

examine.changes_what: A positive survey targets cultures, imaging and source control (line removal, drainage, debridement); a negative survey mandates blood/urine cultures and imaging rather than reassurance.
examine.contraindications: None; do not delay cultures and antibiotics in suspected sepsis while completing the survey.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never let a negative source survey withhold cultures, empiric antibiotics or imaging in a hypotensive, febrile or acutely confused patient with suspected infection.
examine.escalation_warning: Crepitus, bullae, skin necrosis or pain out of proportion (necrotizing fasciitis), a hot joint, peritonism, or purulence at a central line/dialysis catheter in a septic patient require immediate surgical/source-control and line removal decisions.
examine.how: Undress and inspect every line, dialysis and drain/exit site (erythema, purulence, tunnel tenderness), all skin including back, sacrum, heels, perineum, injection sites and wounds; palpate abdomen (peritonism, Murphy sign, flank tenderness), joints and spine for warmth/effusion/tenderness; check urinary catheter, mouth, sinuses, ears and chest. Repeat daily while the source is unknown.
examine.negative_finding: A normal survey does not exclude an occult source: insertion-site inflammation is absent in nearly all catheter-related bloodstream infections, and intra-abdominal, urinary, endovascular and spinal infections are frequently silent in elderly, immunosuppressed or sedated patients.
examine.pitfalls: Line-site appearance has near-zero sensitivity for CRBSI (coagulase-negative staphylococci cause little inflammation); steroids, neutropenia and neuropathy blunt local signs; dressings, obesity and immobility hide sacral, perineal and injection-site infections. Pain out of proportion with unimpressive skin findings suggests necrotizing infection.
examine.positive_finding: Purulence, spreading erythema or tunnel tenderness at a line/exit site, cellulitis or crepitus, a hot swollen joint, peritonism or flank tenderness, or a sacral/heel ulcer with surrounding infection identifies a probable source and directs cultures, source control and empiric therapy.
examine.prerequisites: Full exposure with dressings taken down, adequate lighting and analgesia; review lines, catheters and devices with their insertion dates; log-roll immobile patients to view the sacrum.
examine.rationale: A focused infection source exam can identify other potential sources or complications of infection, guiding immediate management.
examine.title: Focused infection-source exam (line/exit sites, skin, abdomen, joints, sacrum, urine catheter)

examine.changes_what: Positive: adds 1 Wells point and pushes toward compression ultrasound; negative does not stop work-up if other Wells items or D-dimer are positive.
examine.contraindications: None; avoid firm calf compression if DVT is strongly suspected and pain is severe.
examine.do_not_use_when: Do not rely on a negative calf measurement to withhold imaging in a patient with moderate/high Wells probability or with symptoms suggesting PE.
examine.escalation_warning: Massive swelling with cyanosis or pallor and pain (phlegmasia) or a cold pulseless limb requires immediate vascular imaging and consultation.

examine.how: With the patient supine and legs relaxed, mark a point 10 cm below the tibial tuberosity on each leg and measure calf circumference with a tape at the same level bilaterally. A difference >3 cm (symptomatic side larger) is positive; also note localized tenderness along the deep venous system and pitting edema confined to the symptomatic leg.
examine.negative_finding: No calf-diameter difference (LR- 0.57) or no calf swelling (LR- 0.67) lowers the probability of DVT only modestly; it cannot exclude DVT on its own.
examine.pitfalls: Chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema, cellulitis, Baker cyst, and prior DVT produce asymmetry without acute thrombosis; measuring at different levels or in a dependent leg creates spurious differences. Calf tenderness alone has LR near 1.
examine.positive_finding: Calf-diameter difference roughly doubles the odds of DVT (pooled LR+ 1.8); it is the only physical sign with useful rule-in value but is far weaker than the overall Wells score (high probability LR 5.2).
examine.prerequisites: Both legs accessible and comparable (no prior amputation, cast, or chronic unilateral disease that already explains asymmetry).
examine.rationale: Calf asymmetry and tenderness are important for DVT assessment, which must be considered in unilateral leg swelling.
examine.title: Unilateral leg swelling: calf circumference difference >3 cm (10 cm below tibial tuberosity), with calf tenderness

examine.changes_what: A hot swollen joint with painful passive motion should trigger urgent aspiration (cell count, crystals, Gram stain, culture) and orthopedic review; do not treat as cellulitis.
examine.contraindications: Do not force range of motion in a suspected fracture or unstable prosthesis.
examine.do_not_use_when: Never use absence of fever or a modest exam to exclude septic arthritis; prosthetic joints and immunosuppressed patients need aspiration on suspicion alone.
examine.escalation_warning: Hot swollen joint with fever, rigors, sepsis physiology, IV drug use or a prosthesis requires same-day aspiration and orthopedic/ID involvement; delayed treatment destroys the joint.

examine.how: Expose and compare both joints: inspect for swelling and erythema, palpate for warmth and an effusion (patellar tap or bulge sign at the knee, fullness at other joints), then move the joint passively through its range. Note pain with small passive movements, restriction, and whether the patient will bear weight on the limb.
examine.negative_finding: No exam finding rules out septic arthritis; fever is absent in over 40% of cases, and specificity of these findings against gout, pseudogout or reactive arthritis is low.
examine.pitfalls: Cellulitis over a joint, crystal arthritis and hemarthrosis look identical; pain on passive motion favors joint involvement over cellulitis. Elderly, immunosuppressed and prosthetic-joint patients may have muted findings.
examine.positive_finding: An acutely painful, swollen, warm joint with effusion and painful limited passive motion is the expected picture of septic arthritis (joint pain sensitivity 0.85, joint swelling 0.78, fever 0.57) and mandates arthrocentesis before antibiotics.
examine.prerequisites: Adequate exposure of both sides; assess before analgesia blunts findings when feasible.
examine.rationale: A hot, swollen joint with limited motion suggests septic arthritis, which requires urgent aspiration and specialist input.
examine.title: Hot swollen joint with effusion and painful/limited range of motion (refusal to bear weight)
